To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the force generated by the dielectric barrier discharges scales as the square root of the actuator length and that the receptivity of the laminar boundary layer is dominated by the force component with the largest length scale.

the dielectric barrier plasma actuator can be modeled as an array of discrete sources, the force field is compressible, the force is highly directional, and the force is most effective at the leading edge of the actuator and decreases exponentially with downstream distance.

the force generated by the actuation is a function of the Mach number, the Reynolds number and the length scale, and that the most unstable modes are excited by the high-frequency components of the force.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new numerical tool and the application of this tool to the study of the plasma–boundary-layer interactions.
the study of the plasma–compressible-flow coupling mechanisms and their effect on boundary-layer receptivity.
the study of dielectric barrier discharge actuation in a compressible flow and its effect on linear boundary-layer receptivity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the plasma–flow interaction is dominated by the flow Mach number and the length scales of the plasma and the boundary-layer receptivity, while the influence of the Reynolds number is negligible.
the actuator is able to control the transition in the Mach number range from 0 to 2 and for a Reynolds number range of 10 ^{5} to 10 ^{6}.
the compressibility effects are significant for both the dielectric barrier actuator and the receptivity of the boundary layer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, for all cases studied, the dielectric actuator is effective in controlling the boundary layer, but the optimal actuation parameters depend strongly on the Mach number and Reynolds number.
the plasma–flow interaction is strongly dependent on the Mach number of the incoming flow, and that the optimal actuator geometry is a function of the boundary-layer parameters and the Mach number.

the compressibility effects on the plasma force field are not negligible, and the receptivity is significantly affected by compressibility effects, especially for the low- to intermediate-frequency range.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the compressibility of the flow has a significant influence on the receptivity to dielectric barrier discharge actuation.
, for supersonic flows, the actuator length scale is more relevant than the Reynolds number for the control of the receptivity.
the force generated by a DBD actuator is highly compressibility dependent and that the optimal length scale for the actuator is also compressibility dependent.
